messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 35
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Accountant
  trauma_type: Mugging or robbery
  pcl5: 71

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Auditory (Footsteps): Footsteps behind or nearby, Offender Cues: Seeing the offender, Tactile (Unexpected Touch): Being touched unprepared
  Maladaptive Strategies: Self-Blame Rumination: I dwell on what I have done wrong, Dissociate Deliberately: deliberately try to leave my body or blank out, Rumination: Prevention: ruminate about how event could have been prevented
  Threat: Cannot Trust Safety: Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it, Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening, Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place
  Memory: Taste Vividness: I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns, Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred., Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me
  Negative Appraisals: Character Blame: The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place, Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Mele was 35, a married woman of Pacific Islander background who worked as an accountant in a mid-sized office, and by the time she came for treatment she described living as if danger were always just a few seconds away. The event she returned to again and again had happened after an ordinary workday. She had stayed late closing out month-end figures, left the office tired and hungry, and was walking toward her car when she became aware of footsteps behind her in the parking structure. At first she told herself not to overreact, but the sound came faster and closer. Before she could turn properly, a man was on her. She saw his face at close range as he demanded her bag and phone. When he grabbed at her and she felt his hand on her unexpectedly, her body seemed to lock. She remembered the cold concrete smell of the garage, the metallic taste that filled her mouth, and the way she had ended up held in a twisted, braced position while trying not to provoke him. Even now, when the memory returned, her shoulders tightened and her body seemed to fold into that same defensive posture as if the robbery were happening again. Part of what unsettled her was that the scene felt both brutally vivid and strangely unreal; she could describe details of his face and the taste in her mouth, yet would also say that it was so extreme it was hard to believe it had really happened to her.

In the weeks afterward, Mele found herself replaying the robbery in ways that felt punishing and endless. She dwelt on what she had done wrong: why she had stayed late, why she had not asked a coworker to walk with her, why she had not reacted differently when she heard the footsteps. She went over and over how it could have been prevented, as if there must have been one correct decision that would have erased the whole thing. The more she revisited it, the more convinced she became that it had happened because of the sort of person she was—too careless, too slow, too unprepared. Alongside that was a broader conviction that the world itself was dangerous, that what had happened to her was not an exception but proof of how exposed everyone really was.

At work, where she had once been known as steady and meticulous, the environment itself became full of moments she dreaded. If she heard footsteps behind her in the hallway or parking garage, her whole body went rigid before she could think. When a colleague passed too close or touched her shoulder unexpectedly to get her attention, she recoiled, embarrassed and shaken. On one occasion she caught sight of a man near the building entrance whose build and face resembled the offender’s, and she froze long enough that another employee had to ask if she was all right. She began lingering at her desk until others were leaving so she would not walk out alone, then on other days asked her husband to pick her up rather than go to her car by herself. These habits gradually narrowed her routines and made her feel less competent, especially in a job that depended on her being composed and focused.

She also described a constant inability to settle, even in places other people insisted were safe. At home with her husband, with the doors locked, she still could not truly relax. If he was running late and did not answer a text right away, she did not think “traffic” or “busy”; she went immediately to the sense that something bad must be happening. Reassurance did not land. She said that even when people told her she was safe, she could not make herself believe it. Her body remained braced, as if safety were only a story other people could still accept.

When memories surged, Mele sometimes tried deliberately to blank out or leave her body rather than feel what was happening inside her. She described staring into space, going numb on purpose, trying to disappear from herself for a few moments. These episodes frightened her too, because they added to the sense that the robbery had altered something fundamental. She was troubled not only by the memory, but by what she believed it said about her—that she had failed, that her actions had brought it on, that she could not trust either the world or her own judgment.

What finally brought her to treatment was the accumulation of these moments. A coworker had come up behind her at the office and lightly touched her arm while asking a routine question, and Mele jerked away so sharply that she spilled coffee and burst into tears. She was mortified, and later that night she told her husband she could not keep living in a state where footsteps, delays, or a passing resemblance to one man could undo her entire day. Coming in, what frightened her most was the possibility that she would never again feel safe enough to inhabit her own body or move through ordinary places without scanning for danger. What she hoped for, carefully and almost skeptically, was to be able to leave work at the end of the day and believe she was simply going home.
